COMMENTS OF ENGIE NORTH AMERICA INC.  
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, ENGIE North America Inc., (“ENGIE”), 
respectfully submits these comments in response to the filings dated March 24, 2025 of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) (“PJM Filing”), the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, and 
Public Service Gas & Electric made in response to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order 
Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other 
Proceedings (the “Show Cause Order”).1 ENGIE’s comments recognize the significant efforts by 
PJM in its filing while also emphasizing the acute need for clear Commission guidance on co-
location arrangements, the need to safeguard flexibility in PJM’s tariff, and that fairness dictates 
compensating co-location arrangements for benefits provided to the grid.  
 
1  PJM Interconnexion, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025).

3
I. 
COMMUNICATIONS 
All correspondence and communication concerning this filing should be directed to: 
Sarah Bresolin Silver 
Vice President, Government and Regulatory Affairs 
ENGIE North America Inc. 
1360 Post Oak Blvd., Suite 400 
Houston, TX 77056 
sarah.bresolin@engie.com  
 
II. 
INTRODUCTION 
ENGIE North America is a subsidiary of ENGIE SA, based in Paris, France. Globally, 
ENGIE SA is a leading independent power producer, operating 106 GW of installed generation 
capacity, including 38 GW of renewable energy generation throughout 31 countries. ENGIE also 
operates the largest natural gas distribution network in Europe, owns 2,485 miles of transmission 
lines, and is a leading energy supplier globally to commercial and industrial customers.  
With over 2,000 employees in the United States, ENGIE has been actively engaged in the 
domestic power industry for decades. ENGIE operates 12 GW of power generation, primarily 
solar and wind power, and battery energy storage. ENGIE has several major partnerships with 
universities and medical campuses to manage their energy usage and decarbonization efforts and 
operates a large electricity and natural gas supply business for large commercial and industrial 
customers. ENGIE’s retail electricity business leads the way with innovative and integrated 
renewable energy and risk management solutions in 14 retail electric choice markets to 
commercial and industrial customers. ENGIE is also engaged in developing hydrogen projects in 
the Gulf Coast region. ENGIE SA is a partner in the Ocean Winds global joint venture with EDP 
Renewables which is developing offshore wind projects in the United States off the coasts of 
Massachusetts, New York and New Jersey, and California.

4
ENGIE thanks the Commission for initiating the inquiry. Commission perspective and 
direction will provide PJM, market participants and stakeholders with the much-needed certainty 
to pursue and benefit from co-located generation and large load arrangements.  
III. 
COMMENTS 
A. PJM’s filing appropriately acknowledges the acute need for new co-located large 
load and generating facility participation models. 
 
The significant growth of data center, and other large load development, is reshaping the 
energy landscape, driving the need for changes to existing laws and regulations, infrastructure 
development and planning, and electricity market participation arrangements. Although in PJM 
certain frameworks already exist to enable the co-location of large loads and generation, PJM 
correctly recognizes that “clarifications and enhancements could well be in order given that this 
is an evolving area and Tariff provisions did not contemplate the type of arrangements at issue in 
this docket or their implications.”2 
ENGIE agrees. The magnitude and pace at which large loads are seeking to interconnect, 
and the need for new commercial and technical arrangements to satisfy the parties’ diverse 
requirements, portend the creation of new co-location frameworks.  
In addition to confirming PJM’s three existing co-location market participation models, 
PJM’s filing to the Commission’s Show Cause Order includes several potential new options for 
pairing generation with large loads.3 Specifically, new Options 4 through 8 address some key 
aspects of co-location arrangements beyond what is specifically permitted in PJM’s tariff.  
ENGIE appreciates the significant effort that PJM has undergone into conceptualizing 
New Options 4 through 8. ENGIE believes that it is unlikely that meaningful progress can be 
 
2 PJM Interconnection, FERC Case No. EL25-49, at 32, filed March 24, 2025. 
3Id. at 9-20, Att. A.

5
made in meeting the demand for co-locating large loads with generation by leveraging the 
current tools in PJM’s existing tariff. To address the significant increase in requests to 
interconnect large loads co-located with generation, the Commission, PJM and stakeholders must 
explore new and innovative market solutions.  
B. The Commission should provide clear guidance on co-location arrangements.  
In its filing, PJM acknowledges that its efforts “would be greatly assisted by Commission 
guidance.”4  ENGIE agrees and believes that it is essential for the Commission to provide 
guidance on co-location arrangements. Commission guidance would assist PJM market 
participants and stakeholders in obtaining certainty and clarity about available pathways for 
integration of large loads consistent with PJM’s principles. Commission guidance would not just 
provide increased certainty, but it would assist in garnering stakeholder consensus.  
Further, ENGIE recommends that the Commission also investigate and support additional 
co-location arrangements beyond PJM’s options 1 through 8. ENGIE believes that the record 
supports consideration of additional participation options beyond those that already exist and 
those newly proposed. Therefore, ENGIE recommends that the Commission sanction further 
exploration of additional options proposed by stakeholders in comments to the docket. 
C. The Commission must safeguard flexibility in the PJM tariff. 
PJM’s filing outlines eight options for integrating large loads with generating facilities. 
ENGIE acknowledges that these options aim to provide flexibility, clarity and capture multiple 
co-location use cases while ensuring fairness in cost implications and maintaining grid reliability. 
Flexibility in tariff design for meeting the various existing and future co-located configurations is 
 
4 Id. at 32.

6
crucial in the context of co-locating large loads and generating facilities especially in a dynamic 
and rapidly evolving environment. 
First, flexibility will ensure adaptability to changing needs. As data centers, and other 
large loads, grow and their energy needs change, flexible arrangements will help stakeholders 
adapt to evolving demands and technological advancements without major disruptions. For 
example, when needs change, it is foreseeable that shifting between configuration options may 
be more beneficial and efficient. Further, PJM should expect that proposed new options, beyond 
what was conceived in the PJM Proposal, will develop, and must be recognized or enabled by the 
tariff.  
Second, flexibility can also enhance system reliability as configuration design can provide 
multiple pathways for power delivery. Flexibility also allows stakeholders to choose the most 
cost-effective solutions by optimizing the use of, or not, of the electric grid.  
Finally, flexibility in the tariff can help to mitigate future legal and regulatory changes. In 
its submittal, PJM emphasizes that co-located arrangements must comply with state laws and 
regulations.5 Also, that no configuration can be used if it does not comply with state law by 
virtue of it being one of the options.6 Therefore, building flexibility into the tariff language can 
help to navigate the complex regulatory landscapes by offering multiple ways to interconnect.  
D. The Commission must ensure that PJM’s participation options capture and 
recognize the system and ratepayer benefits of co-location. 
 
ENGIE believes that co-location arrangements offer multiple benefits that are shared 
across the co-located load and generating facility, ratepayers, and the electric grid. Such benefits 
should be acknowledged, captured, and where appropriate, compensated in PJM’s tariff.  
 
5 Id. at 3.  
6 Id. at 3-4.

7
While PJM’s submittal states that “participants involved in co-location arrangements 
should pay the costs of any grid services they consume”, PJM does not comment on 
compensating services provided by co-located arrangements to the grid except to express that 
further stakeholder engagement is needed.7 Co-located arrangements can provide cost savings by 
reducing overall system costs which can result in the reduction of costs to ratepayers of 
otherwise interconnecting the load in a non-co-location arrangement. These arrangements can 
also make efficient use of existing transmission and generation resources which can forestall the 
need for new infrastructure investments. Such arrangements may also encourage the 
development of new generating resources which can contribute to increased capacity and grid 
reliability. 
Further, co-located arrangements can offer environmental benefits by encouraging the use 
of renewable energy sources and energy-efficient technologies that will deliver cleaner power to 
the load than the load could draw from the grid.  
Finally, co-located arrangements can offer improved grid reliability and stability. PJM 
addresses the ability of these arrangements to provide back-up service and promises to continue 
to engage with stakeholders to capture potential opportunities.8 Arrangements that provide 
benefits to the grid such as ancillary services, frequency regulation, voltage support, back-up 
service or blackstart capability, should be compensated for providing those benefits like any 
other market participant.  
 
 
 
 
7 Id. at 68. 
8 Id. at 69-70.

8
E. The Commission should address several outstanding issues to ensure 
implementation of co-location options.  
 
Although PJM’s Proposal touches on interconnection of co-located arrangements, PJM’s 
response is brief and does not capture some of the outstanding stakeholder questions or 
concerns.9 For example, currently the load and generation interconnection study processes are 
bifurcated. Entities wishing to take advantage of colocation require clarity as to how the 
arrangements will be studied. ENGIE recommends that the Commission and PJM explore 
whether efficiencies can be gained by studying co-location arrangements in an alternative 
manner, such as evaluating the net impact on the grid, which recognizes the co-located nature of 
the interconnection request.  
ENGIE also notes the complexity of this type of study including potential mismatching of 
the time when the load and the generation come online or the lifetime of the load versus the 
lifetime of the generation or the variances of operational characteristics of co-located load and 
generation. ENGIE encourages the Commission and PJM to address these difficult but critical 
questions and concepts to enable the rapid integration of co-located arrangements.  
Further, ENGIE notes that the Commission requested information from PJM on how co-
location arrangements may provide benefits.10  While PJM did not respond substantively to this 
request, PJM acknowledges that further engagement is needed. ENGIE recommends that the 
Commission require that PJM evaluate the benefits of co-located arrangements and design a joint 
and expedited interconnection review process for large load and generation as well as a 
compensation framework that fairly compensates the facilities for the services they provide.  
 
 
9 Id. at 32-34. 
10 Id. at 70.

9
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
ENGIE commends the Commission for its continued interest and inquiry into co-located 
arrangements. We also recognize and appreciate the significant work that PJM has accomplished  
in its filing to the Commission. ENGIE encourages the Commission to consider and take action 
on our recommendations. We look forward to engaging further with the Commission, PJM and 
stakeholders as the opportunity arises.  
 
 
Respectfully Submitted, 
 
/s/ Sarah Bresolin Silver 
Sarah Bresolin Silver 
ENGIE North America Inc. 
1360 Post Oak Blvd. 
Houston, TX 77056 
sarah.bresolin@engie.com
